question: A 43-year-old man hospitalized for acute pancreatitis develops a high-grade fever and productive cough with gelatinous sputum. A sample of his expectorated sputum is obtained and fixed to a microscope slide using heat. A crystal violet dye is applied to the slide, followed by an iodine solution, acetone solution, and lastly, safranin dye. A photomicrograph of the result is shown. Which of the following cell components is responsible for the pink color seen on this stain?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Heat fixation of sputum sample" -> "Crystal violet dye binds to cell components" -> "Iodine solution applied" -> "Acetone solution used as decolorizer" -> "Safranin dye applied as counterstain" -> "Peptidoglycan retains crystal violet-iodine complex" -> "Mycolic acid does not retain crystal violet" -> "Capsular polysaccharide does not retain crystal violet" -> "Peptidoglycan appears purple, other components washed out" -> "Safranin stains components not retaining crystal violet" -> "Capsular polysaccharide stained pink by safranin" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Heat fixation of sputum sample" -> "Application of crystal violet" -> "Binding of crystal violet to gram-positive bacteria" -> "Iodine treatment forms crystal violet-iodine complex" -> "Acetone decolorizes non-peptidoglycan components" -> "Safranin used as counterstain" -> "Non-peptidoglycan components take up safranin" -> "Capsular polysaccharide stained pink by safranin" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Sputum sample fixed and stained" -> "Crystal violet stains gram-positive cells" -> "Iodine fixes the stain" -> "Acetone removes unstabilized crystal violet" -> "Safranin stains cells not retaining crystal violet" -> "Mycolic acid resistant to crystal violet" -> "Protein does not specifically retain crystal violet" -> "Glycogen does not retain stains" -> "Capsular polysaccharide absorbs safranin, appears pink" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Preparation of sputum slide" -> "Crystal violet applied to bacteria" -> "Iodine solution stabilizes the dye on thick cell walls" -> "Acetone strips dye from cells with thinner walls" -> "Safranin applied as secondary stain" -> "Peptidoglycan retains primary stain, not relevant here" -> "Mycolic acid not present in all bacteria" -> "Protein and glycogen do not retain dyes specifically" -> "Capsular polysaccharide picks up safranin, turns pink" -> 95%
analysis: The staining procedure described in the question is the Gram stain, a common method used to differentiate bacteria into two groups based on the composition of their cell walls. The crystal violet dye and iodine solution form a complex that gets trapped within the thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria, which is then decolorized by the acetone solution. Gram-negative bacteria, which have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane, do not retain the violet-iodine complex and are instead stained pink by the safranin counterstain. Therefore, the pink color observed in the photomicrograph indicates the presence of Gram-negative bacteria, highlighting their thinner peptidoglycan layer.
